title: Kumbhakarna and tamas
hookLine: Ravana loses his first duel, and orders the giant who sleeps for months to be woken
carry: kumbhakarna is tamas: the sleep that misses what matters

cards: Ravana finally rides out himself. He strikes Lakshmana down with a great spear and tries to lift him to carry him off, and can't move him. Hanuman can, easily, and carries Lakshmana to safety.
Then Rama meets Ravana, smashes his chariot, and cuts the crown from his head. And Rama stops. You've fought hard today, he says, and you're tired.
Go home and rest. Come back tomorrow, and see what I can do. Ravana goes home alive, beaten, humiliated.
And he gives an order: wake my brother.

teach.b: Ravana's brother is Kumbhakarna, and his name says it: pot-ears. He's a giant beyond giants, and he sleeps. Not for a night.
For months. Waking him is a comic set piece in the war book. Rakshasas pile up mountains of food beside him.
They beat drums and blow conches by his ears, hit him with clubs, and march elephants over his body. Nothing. Finally he yawns, stretches, and wakes up hungry.

Why does he sleep like that? Valmiki gives two answers. In one, Brahma, the creator, cursed the greedy young giant to sleep as if dead, then softened it at Ravana's pleading: six months asleep, one day awake.

teach.h: A CURSE, OR A TWISTED BOON.
teach.b: In the other, as Kumbhakarna was about to ask Brahma for a boon, the goddess Sarasvati entered his speech, and the boon he asked for was sleep. Hindu teachers have long seen more than a joke here.
The Bhagavad Gita names three gunas, three strands woven through everything, our minds included: sattva, clarity; rajas, restless wanting; and tamas, heaviness.
Tamas, it says, binds us through carelessness, laziness and sleep.
Many teachers read Lanka's three brothers as those three strands: Ravana, all wanting; Vibhishana, clear; and Kumbhakarna, tamas, asleep while his own city fights for its life.
In many Indian homes, a teenager who sleeps till noon gets called Kumbhakarna.

teach.h: TAMAS: THE SLEEP THAT MISSES WHAT MATTERS.
teach.b: It's a tease, and a teaching: the heaviness in us can sleep straight through what matters, until something shakes it awake.

how: The waking of Kumbhakarna is a favorite scene in Ramlila and in shadow-puppet traditions, often played for laughs; in many Indian families a heavy sleeper is teasingly called Kumbhakarna.

s: Rama kills Ravana in their first duel
he breaks his chariot and crown, then sends him home to rest.
Valmiki gives two different reasons for Kumbhakarna's sleep
a curse from Brahma in the Yuddha Kanda, a twisted boon in the Uttara Kanda.
many teachers read Kumbhakarna as tamas, one of the Gita's three gunas
Ravana as rajas, Vibhishana as sattva, Kumbhakarna as tamas: a reading, not Valmiki's own words.

games.q: finals week. you've slept through two alarms and three study plans. by the teaching of the gunas, what lifts tamas?
o: more sleep. it'll pass on its own.
light, getting up, and one clear thing to do.
feeling guilty about it until it changes.
games.why: the Gita ties tamas to carelessness, laziness and sleep. it lifts the way Kumbhakarna woke: something shakes it, and you get up and act.

practice: Sit up tall, the opposite of a sleeper, and let light into your eyes. Take three deep breaths that wake the body.
If you pray, you might whisper the close of the Gayatri, the morning prayer many Hindus say: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, may that light stir our minds.
If you don't, name one thing you've been sleeping through, and set it in front of you for today.

wordCard.voice: Kumbhakarna. Ravana's giant brother, pot-ears, who sleeps for months, and whom many teachers read as tamas, the heaviness that sleeps through what matters.

orig.note: Sanskrit Kumbhakarṇa: from kumbha, pot or jar, and karṇa, ear.

carryVoice: Your line: kumbhakarna is tamas, the sleep that misses what matters. Awake now, the giant has something to tell his brother. Day six hundred forty-five.
